# Richard Stallman: Concise Summary
Richard Stallman, born in 1953 in New York City, was immersed in computer programming from a young age and became an influential figure in the hacker community while at Harvard University and the MIT AI Laboratory. He contributed to projects such as TECO, Emacs, and Lisp machine operating systems, and was noted for his opposition to restricted access and proprietary software. Experiencing firsthand the rise of software copyright and restrictions, Stallman advocated for the rights of users to freely use, study, share, and modify software, viewing proprietary limitations as unethical. In 1983, he founded the GNU project to develop a free Unix-like operating system, later establishing the Free Software Foundation (FSF) in 1985. He originated the concept of "copyleft" and authored essential GNU tools—including Emacs, GCC, and GDB—and popularized the term "GNU/Linux" for operating systems using the Linux kernel and GNU tools.
Stallman's activism extends beyond programming to software freedom, digital rights, copyright reform, and surveillance resistance. He is a prolific writer and speaker, known for distinguishing free software from open source, and for insisting on correct terminology. Stallman has received numerous honors, including the MacArthur Fellowship, Grace Murray Hopper Award, and several honorary doctorates. His leadership in the FSF and the GNU project has been pivotal, though he has faced controversy and temporarily resigned from official positions in 2019, later returning to the FSF board in 2021. Stallman continues to reside in Massachusetts, actively advocating for digital freedom and receiving treatment for follicular lymphoma as of 2023.
